## Proof Placement

### Sotheby's
- Sports memorabilia claim ("From Pele to Michael Jordan...") is in the body copy of the Sports Week section. Same section, no external source.
- Estimate values ("150,000 - 220,000 USD") are displayed on individual lot cards. Same card where item appears.
- Auction dates and locations are metadata on each lot. Same card.
- Consignment claim ("Our estimate tool offers a simple way...") is in the estimate tool hero. Same block.

### Aesop
- "Meticulous attention to detail" claim is in brand statement. Not independently proven on homepage.
- Sensory product descriptions (scent, texture, feeling) are on individual product pages, not abstract promises on homepage.
- Educational content (essays, podcasts) demonstrated via The Library section link. Proof exists but is one click away.

### Klim
- Typeface usage claims demonstrated via Fonts in Use section with real client work shown. Same page, but requires scrolling/clicking to see.
- "Die Grotesk shaped in the long shadow of Helvetica" claim is in blog post. Must navigate to blog to verify.

## Claim Qualification

### Sotheby's (How claims are constructed)
- All major transaction claims are qualified with specifics: specific athletes, specific estimate ranges, specific dates/times, specific locations
- Claims use "offer" language ("Our estimate tool offers a simple way...") + direct user benefit
- No superlatives; instead: direct comparison ("From Pele to Michael Jordan to Victor Wembanyama, the auctions offer a wide variety...")
- Newsletter copy is minimal action-focused: "Receive the best from Sotheby's delivered to your inbox"

### Aesop (How claims are constructed)
- Product claims avoid clinical language; instead emphasize sensory experience
- Brand positioning claims (meticulous, effica, sensory pleasure) are stated once in brand statement, not repeated
- Educational content framed as resource hub, not as proof of expertise
- Use of "formulations created with..." language (process-oriented, not result-oriented)

### Klim (How claims are constructed)
- No abstract claims about quality; instead demonstrate via real work examples
- Blog posts frame design philosophy as narrative, not assertion ("Die Grotesk was shaped in the long shadow of Helvetica, a typeface both revered and resented...")
- Fonts in Use section provides evidence-based positioning (client + project count)

## Conversion Path

### Sotheby's
- First ask: Browse auctions (view, bid, register as bidder)
- Second ask: Sell items (request estimate, consign)
- Third ask: Email signup (newsletter)
- User gets first: Auction catalog access, product browsing (immediate value)
- Transaction friction: Bidding requires account/authentication (not shown on homepage)
- Newsletter offer: General content summary

### Aesop
- First ask: Browse products by category (skin, hair, fragrance)
- Second ask: Read education/stories (The Library, The Fabulist)
- Third ask: Email signup (newsletter)
- User gets first: Product discovery + sensory descriptions (immediate aesthetic value)
- Transaction friction: Checkout is one-page (low friction once products selected)
- Newsletter offer: General brand news

### Klim
- First ask: Browse font families (view, preview, buy)
- Second ask: Read design content (blog, Fonts in Use)
- Third ask: Email signup (newsletter)
- User gets first: Font preview and usage examples (immediate design reference value)
- Transaction friction: Purchase requires account (not shown on homepage)
- Newsletter offer: Font news and releases

## Distinctive (One thing they do that nobody else does)

### Sotheby's
Combination of auction (time-gated scarcity) + retail (fixed price) + content (editorial storytelling) on single homepage. Most competitors isolate these functions. Sotheby's treats the page as a unified marketplace where a user can bid on sports memorabilia, purchase a Hermès handbag, and read an article about 250 years of American art in the same session. The tabbed auction interface (Americas/Europe/Asia) is also distinctive: it lets users filter by geography without page reload.

### Aesop
Sensory product language as primary differentiator. Instead of "10ml bottle, 5% retinol," the site emphasizes scent, texture, and emotional effect. The Fabulist (literary magazine) as brand extension is distinctive. Most skincare sites have blog content; Aesop launched a full literary journal. This positions the brand as cultural, not transactional.

### Klim
Fonts in Use as built-in case study gallery on the homepage. Most type foundries link to external showcases; Klim embedded real-world applications directly in the product discovery flow. User can see Die Grotesk applied to actual architecture projects before clicking Buy. This collapses research and purchase into one space.

## Noise (One thing they do that is category noise)

### Sotheby's
Heavy use of featured collection tiles with placeholder images (SVG placeholders for lazy loading). The technique is functional but reads as standard e-commerce. Nearly every lot in the highlights section has a muted color tile + text overlay. This is noise because it dilutes the page hierarchy; every item competes visually at the same weight.

### Aesop
Shoppable navigation (product reveal on hover) is sophisticated but also noise. It solves a technical problem (quick restock for loyalists) but adds invisible interaction logic. New users don't discover it. The case study notes this was validated via user testing, but it's still adding complexity to an otherwise minimal aesthetic.

### Klim
Newsletter signup copy "Get news about our fonts" is standard noise. Every foundry site has a newsletter. The phrasing is utilitarian, not distinctive. It doesn't explain what value the user gets (new release alerts, design tips, behind-the-scenes content). Missed opportunity in a site otherwise focused on education and community.

## Summary: What Makes a Light Page Read as Expensive

Not whitespace quantity (all three use generous margins). The delimiter is:

1. **Copy precision.** Sotheby's uses exact lot numbers, specific athletes, date-time stamps. Aesop uses texture/scent language, not spec sheets. Klim uses client names and case counts. None waste words on superlatives. Vague language (best, finest, premium) reads cheap; specific language (15 July 2026, ZRS Arkitekten, Founders Grotesk) reads expensive.

2. **Typeface restraint.** Aesop uses 3 typefaces across system (Optima + Suisse Int'l + Zapf Humanist). Sotheby's appears to use 1 sans-serif system. Klim uses its own typeface family. Cheaper sites use 5+ typefaces. Constraint signals confidence.

3. **Proof placement.** Klim shows Fonts in Use. Sotheby's shows lot estimates. Aesop shows sensory product descriptions on each product. Claims are demonstrated, not asserted. Cheap sites assert (we are the best), expensive sites show (here is what we built).

4. **Product density varies.** Sotheby's homepage shows ~11 highlights + 30+ upcoming auctions in tabbed view (high density, but organized). Klim shows ~20 typeface families (collections grouped). Aesop implies lower density (focus on seasonal/featured). But all three use card or grid structure with consistent spacing, not maxed-out layouts.

5. **Section labeling.** All three use 2-4 word section labels. No marketing speak (Discover Endless Possibilities, Explore Our World). The labels name the job (Highlights Closing Soon, Fonts in Use, Upcoming Auctions).

Result: these sites read expensive because they respect user time (precise copy, clear structure, labeled sections) and show evidence (typeface pairings, case studies, lot data) rather than assert.
